problem: Vanilla ViTs used as drop-in replacements for ResNets in end-to-end (model-free) visual navigation agents underperform. From scratch, ViT-Small gets 36.1% SR vs 59.9% for a half-width ResNet50 on ImageNav, and ViT agents do not improve when scaled up. Meanwhile, the strongest ObjectNav/ImageNav systems rely on task-specific modules (depth, segmentation, detectors, semantic maps, planners).
motivation: General-purpose agents built from task-agnostic components (ViT, conv, LSTM) are simpler, apply to many tasks, and should scale positively with compute (the 'bitter lesson'). However, the recipe for training ViTs inside navigation policies is brittle and largely undiscovered. The authors observe that the [CLS] token and global average pooling discard the spatial layout of patches, which navigation needs. They also find that the widely used ZER reward can be hacked once agents are strong enough.
key_idea: Use an in-domain MAE-pretrained ViT whose patch tokens are reshaped into a grid and compressed by a 3×3 conv, instead of CLS/avg-pooling, inside a plain ViT+LSTM policy. Combine this with policy-training fixes (no AvgPool downsampling, a low encoder learning rate, augmentations, and a potential-based fix of the ZER angle reward) to get a simple SoTA baseline for ImageNav and ObjectNav.
insight: Keeping spatial structure is what makes ViTs work for navigation. From scratch, the compression layer lifts ViT-Small from 36.1 SR ([CLS]) / 35.0 (GAP) to 67.4, beating ResNet50's 59.9 (Tab. 2). With pretraining, the compression layer still gives +5.1 SR over GAP (82.0 vs 76.9) at similar SPL (Tab. 7b), which the authors attribute to better goal recognition and stopping. Positive scaling only appears with in-domain SSL pretraining: from scratch, ViT-Small→ViT-Base drops SR 67.4→65.0, while MAE-pretrained goes 80.5→82.0 SR and 55.2→58.7 SPL (Tab. 3). Fine-tuning details dominate. A default encoder LR (2.5e-4) gives 51.0 SR, worse than a frozen encoder at 61.8, while a tuned 1.5e-6 gives 82.0 (Tab. 7c). Removing augmentations drops SR by 24.2. Removing the AvgPool that prior agents apply to input images adds +32.9 SR (Tab. 1). The ZER reward is hackable (agents re-enter the goal radius repeatedly to farm the angle reward); a potential-based angle term fixes it (82.0/58.7 vs 76.5/44.1 SR/SPL, Tab. 4). In-domain SSL (MAE or Data2Vec) far outperforms CLIP, whether frozen (51.7 SR) or fine-tuned (65.5 SR).
method: Visual encoder: ViT-Small or ViT-Base on 16×16 patches of the RGB observation, pretrained with MAE (75% masking, 800 epochs) on the in-domain HGSP dataset. HGSP has 1.45M 512×512 images from oracle shortest-path trajectories in 800 HM3D + 72 Gibson training scenes. The encoder is fine-tuned end-to-end with a small tuned learning rate (1.5e-6 for ImageNav, 1e-4 for ObjectNav).

Compression layer: ViT patch tokens are reshaped to an H×W grid, passed through a 3×3 Conv + GroupNorm(1) + ReLU that reduces channels so the flattened output is about 2048-d, then flattened. This preserves spatial layout instead of using the [CLS] token or global average pooling; an FC layer follows.

Policy: visual features are concatenated with a goal embedding (and, for ObjectNav, a GPS+Compass encoding) and fed to an LSTM that outputs discrete actions. For ImageNav the goal image uses a replicated visual encoder pipeline; for ObjectNav the category uses a learned embedding.

Corrected ImageNav reward: the ZER angle-shaping term is replaced by a difference of potentials θ̂_{t-1}−θ̂_t, with θ̂_t = angle-to-goal inside the goal radius and π outside. Reward gained inside the radius is fully lost on exit (zero-sum), which prevents reward hacking. Terms are success c_s=5 and stop-facing-goal c_a=5 (θ_g=25°), plus distance shaping and slack penalty 0.01.

Training recipe: ImageNav uses DD-PPO for 500M steps on Gibson with 320 environments and no AvgPool downsampling of input images. ObjectNav uses distributed behavior cloning on 77k Habitat-Web human demonstrations (~12.1M steps), trained for ~400M steps with 512 environments.
Data augmentation during training and at test time: color jitter (0.3 for ImageNav, 0.4 for ObjectNav) followed by random shifts (pad 4 or 16), applied consistently across time.

numbers_note: ImageNav uses the Mem-Aug Nav Gibson ImageNav benchmark; its validation set (14 scenes, 4,200 episodes) serves as the eval split. The paper reports the checkpoint with the highest val SR (ImageNav) or val SPL (ObjectNav), so val numbers involve checkpoint selection on the eval set. The ViT size used for ObjectNav is not stated explicitly (the paper says the same pretrained encoder is used for both tasks). Reward-hacking curves (Fig. 5) and the failure breakdown (Fig. 6) appear only in figures.
results: On Gibson ImageNav, OVRL-V2 (ViT-Base + MAE + compression layer) reaches 82.0 SR / 58.7 SPL with a single RGB camera. That is +27.8 SR over the previous single-camera SoTA OVRL (54.2) and +13.0 SR over the 4-camera Mem-Aug Nav (69.0). On HM3D ObjectNav Test-Standard it gets 64.0 SR / 29.0 SPL (val 64.7 / 28.1) using only RGB + GPS+Compass. It beats Stretch/SemExp (60.0 SR), Habitat-Web (55.0) and ProcTHOR (54.0), and is 1 point behind the concurrent PIRLNav (65.0). Its SPL is lower than modular and RL-finetuned methods (Stretch 34.0, PIRLNav 33.0).
limitations: ObjectNav path efficiency is weak: SPL 29.0 vs 34.0 for depth+semantic-map methods. The agent is trained only by imitation of human demos, with no RL fine-tuning; the authors suggest PIRLNav-style RL fine-tuning could help.

Results are sensitive to the fine-tuning recipe: a badly chosen encoder LR is worse than a frozen encoder, and removing augmentations drops SR by 24.2. Both ablations and the failure analysis are on ImageNav only. Reported numbers come from the best checkpoint on the validation set.

Simulation only, with no real-robot validation. About 6% of ImageNav val goals are semantically meaningless ('bad goals'), capping success near 94%; other failures ('unexplained stop', 'looked similar', 'nearly reached') remain.
